passage: From my bench by the park gate I watched two children argue over the one swing. The girl called Indu said to Suraj, "You push me, then I push you." Suraj frowned and looked at the swing, then nodded. Indu climbed on and he pushed. She counted out loud to ten. They swapped: Suraj sat and Indu pushed, counting to ten again, a little louder. Neither looked cross at the end. I could not tell whether Suraj really liked the deal, but he stayed and played until the light went.

qa.q: How high did Indu count on each turn?
qa.a: Indu counted out loud to ten.

qa.q: What might Suraj be feeling when he frowns and looks at the swing before nodding?
qa.a: He may be unsure at first, weighing the offer, and then accept it as fair. The narrator cannot know for certain.

qa.q: What other approach could work if Suraj had said no, and why?
qa.a: They could ask a grown-up nearby to set a fair turn for each. An adult can settle it when two children cannot agree.

qa.q: How does the exchange look to the narrator on the bench?
qa.a: The narrator sees two children sort it out fairly on their own. The narrator also admits not knowing how Suraj really felt.

grounding: A child proposes taking turns pushing, and both children get a fair, counted turn on the swing.
